message.content:
You are an adversarial deep-tech investor. EXECUTION skeptic: can a tiny team starting with software today actually reach a sellable product? Attack capital needs, hiring, sales cycle, technical risk.
Default to skepticism; score 1-10 where 7+ means you would actually take a meeting. Thesis:
{
  "name": "Kelvin Light (athermal high-efficiency multi-wavelength laser source)",
  "one_liner": "The bold bet: kill the TEC — an uncooled, high-power, multi-wavelength external laser source that attacks the single largest power and reliability sink in every optical link.",
  "wedge": "An ELSFP-form-factor external laser module built around uncooled/athermal multi-wavelength emission (quantum-dot gain, which tolerates 80°C uncooled operation, and/or comb generation) plus zero-static-power wavelength stabilization (photoconductive/PCM-assisted locking instead of brute-force thermoelectric cooling). Target spec: cut ELS wall-plug power 40-60% versus today's DFB+TEC modules at the ~24.5dBm launch powers CPO links require. Sold into the standardized socket the OIF ELSFP and OCI MSA just guaranteed — first customers are CPO switch/system builders (Broadcom ecosystem partners, Celestial/Marvell-class XPU programs) and the hyperscalers who wrote the standards.",
  "why_now": "The pain is quantified and public: Meta says ~90% of optical link failures trace to lasers and lasers consume ~60% of link power; lasers+TECs are ~70% of ELS power draw. NVIDIA just paid $4B into Coherent/Lumentum purely for laser supply security — the demand side is desperate. The socket is standardized (ELSFP-02.0, Jan 2025; OCI MSA WDM, Mar 2026), so a component startup doesn't need to win an architecture war. The enabling pieces matured independently: QD-on-Si epi supply chains exist (Quintessent/IQE), Tower/OpenLight offer open-foundry gain integration, comb sources are productizing (Xscape FalconX 8λ), and heaterless ring locking was demonstrated (NewPhotonics). Nobody has assembled 'uncooled + multi-λ + high power + ELSFP' into one module — every light-source startup is attacking a different sub-problem.",
  "market": "Lasers/light sources are the largest BOM and power line item in a CPO market going from $46M (2024) to $8-10B (2030), plus the pluggable market (~$26B datacom optics in 2026) where LPO's power story makes efficient lasers equally valuable. If ELS modules are 15-25% of CPO system value, the light-source TAM is $1.5-2.5B by 2030; a startup with a differentiated module taking 10-15% share is a $200-400M revenue business — and the NVIDIA/Coherent/Lumentum dynamic shows laser suppliers now command strategic (not component) valuations.",
  "competition": "The most crowded deep-tech lane in the sector, be clear-eyed: Coherent and Lumentum (now NVIDIA-capitalized with purchase commitments — they own today's sockets); the funded startup cohort each holding one piece — Xscape (combs, $81M, Cisco+NVIDIA backing), OpenLight (integrated InP, $84M), Scintil ($58M, NVIDIA), Quintessent (QD, Tower), Aylight (ETH, multiwavelength); Broadcom's internal ELS. Your differentiation must be the system-level power number (module wall-plug efficiency at spec launch power, uncooled), not a device physics claim — if you can't beat Lumentum's next-gen module by >30% in qualified testing, this company shouldn't exist.",
  "moat": "Hard-won physics and reliability data: uncooled high-power operation with telecom-grade wavelength stability is a genuine multi-year materials/photonics problem (QD gain dynamics, athermal cavity design, locking electronics), and the resulting qualification corpus (HTOL hours, FIT rates — Intel's 0.09 FIT benchmark is the bar) is the true barrier; hyperscalers qualify lasers over years and don't switch casually. Patents on the athermal stabilization architecture matter here more than in software theses. Post-qualification, laser sockets are among the stickiest in hardware.",
  "capital_intensity": "High and unavoidable — this is the deep-tech play: III-V epi runs, hybrid integration development, reliability labs (burn-in racks, HTOL chambers), and 3-4 module generations. ~$15-20M seed/A to a working prototype module (leveraging Tower/OpenLight and IQE-style epi supply rather than owning a fab), $80-150M cumulative through hyperscaler qualification and early production. Comparable trajectory: Xscape at $81M pre-production. Non-negotiable: an NVIDIA/Cisco/hyperscaler strategic in the round, both for validation and for the qualification fast-path.",
  "software_mvp": "This week (genuinely useful, not decoration): a laser reliability and link-power modeling platform — physics-based FIT-rate and wavelength-drift models fit to published data (Intel's 45,000-hour HTOL corpus, Meta's failure statistics), plus an ELS power-budget optimizer that shows hyperscalers exactly what an uncooled architecture saves across a 100K-GPU fabric. It sharpens your own spec targets, generates design-partner conversations a year before hardware exists, and its telemetry/health-prediction module becomes the firmware companion product (laser fleet monitoring) once modules ship.",
  "risks": [
    "Physics failure mode: uncooled operation may not reach the power+linewidth+stability corner CPO needs; QD output power per wavelength remains the known weakness",
    "Reliability qualification takes 2-3 years of accumulated hours no amount of money compresses — the market may lock in Lumentum/Coherent sockets first, especially with NVIDIA's purchase commitments steering volume",
    "Crowded cap tables: five funded startups plus two NVIDIA-backed incumbents means acquirer supply may exhaust before your exit window",
    "InP/GaAs epi supply chain concentration (China exposure on InP substrates) adds geopolitical input risk",
    "Capital markets risk: this needs $100M+ across a window where photonics funding is hostage to the AI capex cycle; a 2027 AI-spending pause strands the company mid-qualification",
    "Team risk: requires world-class III-V materials + photonics + reliability engineering simultaneously — perhaps 200 people on earth qualify, mostly at Intel/Lumentum/UCSB"
  ]
}

- doc-extraction: CRE Brochure Data Extraction
- slack:channel-digest: Get a digest of recent activity across multiple Slack channels
- slack:draft-announcement: Draft a well-formatted Slack announcement and save it as a draft
- slack:find-discussions: Find discussions about a specific topic across Slack channels
- slack:standup: Generate a standup update based on your recent Slack activity
- slack:summarize-channel: Summarize recent activity in a Slack channel
- slack:block-kit: Help developers build and validate Block Kit layouts for Slack messages, modals, and Home tabs. Provides authoritative block references and validates with the blocks.validate API. Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels). Also trigger when they mention "blocks", "Block Kit Builder", or paste JSON containing block structures like `"type": "section"`.
- slack:create-slack-app: Guide developers through creating a Slack app or agent using the Slack CLI and Bolt (JS or Python). Handles prerequisites, sandbox setup, authentication, project creation from templates, and local development.
- slack:slack-api: Discover, navigate, and call Slack Web API methods (the family.method endpoints at slack.com/api like chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.info, views.open). Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. This skill covers the Web API method layer: finding the right method, reading its contract (scopes, arguments, errors), and calling it over raw HTTP with curl or through a Slack SDK.
- slack:slack-cli: Use the Slack CLI to create, run, and manage Slack apps from the terminal. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest); or when searching the Slack developer documentation for any topic (socket mode, the Events API, OAuth, manifests, Bolt).
- slack:slack-messaging: Guidance for composing well-formatted, effective Slack messages using standard markdown
- slack:slack-search: Guidance for effectively searching Slack to find messages, files, channels, and people
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.rationale: Well-researched sector memo, but it fails the mandate on its own admissions: a tiny team starting with software cannot execute this. The software MVP (reliability/link-power modeling fit to Intel's and Meta's published data) is non-revenue decoration that derisks nothing — hyperscaler qual teams won't credit models built on other companies' device data, and the 'firmware companion product' requires shipped modules that are 5+ years away. The real company needs $15-20M pre-prototype, $80-150M through qualification, and a hiring pool the thesis itself sizes at ~200 people worldwide, before a single dollar of revenue around 2031 — while CPO ELS sockets are being qualified 2025-2027 with NVIDIA purchase commitments steering volume to Coherent/Lumentum and seven funded competitors ($60-500M each) already ahead. Comparable trajectory isn't Xscape at $81M; it's Ayar Labs' SuperNova at roughly half a billion and still pre-volume. The kill criterion (>30% better than Lumentum next-gen in qualified testing) can't be measured until ~$50M is spent. Honest risk section and correct system-level framing earn it a 3 instead of a 2, but I would not take this meeting without a named ex-Intel/Lumentum/UCSB laser-reliability founder and a committed strategic — both absent.
fatal_flaws: Software-first premise is false on the thesis's own terms: the MVP modeling platform has no standalone revenue, no proprietary data (it fits Intel/Meta published numbers), and no credibility with qualification teams — this is a $100M+ hardware company from day one wearing a software costume.

Internal physics contradiction: TECs exist largely FOR reliability (junction temperature drives FIT via Arrhenius), so promising uncooled 80°C operation AND Intel-class 0.09 FIT AND 24.5 dBm launch power from QD gain (whose per-wavelength power is the admitted weakness) stacks three unsolved problems multiplicatively; the PCM/photoconductive locking scheme is TRL-2/3 with unqualified endurance and drift.

Timeline vs. window: software start today puts a prototype at ~2028-29 and qualification at ~2031, while the standardized ELSFP/OCI sockets are being qualified 2025-2027 with NVIDIA purchase commitments locking volume to Coherent/Lumentum — the 'standard socket' advantage equally benefits seven funded incumbents/startups already 2-4 years ahead.

Capital comparables are understated: the closest analog to an external multi-wavelength CPO light source (Ayar Labs' SuperNova) has consumed ~$500M and is still pre-volume; $15-20M to a working ELSFP prototype (module packaging, pump/control electronics, hybrid QD integration, burn-in infrastructure) is not credible.

No founder and no strategic: the thesis names a hyperscaler/NVIDIA strategic as 'non-negotiable' and identifies a ~200-person global talent pool, then provides neither — the two items that would actually earn a meeting.

Falsification comes too late: the company's own kill criterion (beat Lumentum next-gen by >30% wall-plug at spec launch power, uncooled, in qualified testing) cannot be tested before roughly $50M and 3-4 years are spent.
improvements: Recast entirely around a founding team that brings the qualification corpus with them (e.g., ex-Intel silicon photonics laser reliability leadership with HTOL/FIT track record) — in this sector the team IS the thesis; without a named founder the memo is unactionable.

Replace the software MVP with a real de-risking milestone: a funded JDA or paid NRE with one CPO system builder (Broadcom ecosystem partner or XPU program) to characterize uncooled QD gain at spec power on Tower/OpenLight MPW runs within 12 months and <$3M, giving an early physics kill-switch before the module build.

Resolve the TEC/reliability contradiction with data or a hedge: quantify expected FIT at 80°C junction temp from published QD activation energies, or reposition as 'reduced-cooling' (passive heatsink, no TEC) rather than fully uncooled, which preserves most of the power win at lower physics risk.

Consider the licensing/IP-core exit path explicitly: if the athermal stabilization architecture is the real asset, a 20-person company licensing to Lumentum/Coherent/Broadcom at $30-50M raised is a far more executable plan than fighting them for module sockets at $150M raised.

Sequence a nearer-revenue wedge: sell the wavelength-locking chip/electronics subsystem (the zero-static-power stabilization) to existing ELS module makers as a component in 2027, funding the full-module ambition with revenue and design-in relationships.

Name the strategic and the qual path in the round construction: which hyperscaler co-authored the ELSFP spec will sponsor accelerated qualification, and what purchase-commitment structure offsets NVIDIA's commitments to incumbents — without this the 2030 market-lock risk is dispositive.
